etymologies.etymologyHTML: From loose +‎ -en.

quote.citation: 1626, Francis Bacon, Sylva Sylvarum: or A Naturall Historie, London: William Lee, Century 5, p. 111,[1]
quote.text: […]  after a yeares Rooting, then Shaking doth the Tree good, by Loosening of the Earth  […]

quote.citation: 1944 May and June, “The Why and the Wherefore: Locomotive Soot Blowers”, in Railway Magazine, page 194:
quote.text: In order to deal with deposits of soot on boiler-tubes while running, especially if poor coal is in use, locomotives are often now provided with blowers on the firebox back-plate which can be made to discharge a jet of high pressure steam towards the firebox tubeplates; this has the effect of loosening and blowing off the soot deposits.

quote.citation: 1960 December, “Talking of Trains: The railways and the Devon floods”, in Trains Illustrated, page 709:
quote.text: [...] and on the Saturday heavy seas pounded the W.R. on its exposed coastal stretch between Dawlish and Teignmouth, loosening the ballast and forcing trains to proceed with extreme caution.

quote.citation: 1992, Michael Ondaatje, chapter 10, in The English Patient‎[2], London: Picador, published 1993, page 265:
quote.text: His days at the villa had loosened his body and freed his tenseness  […]

quote.citation: 1630, Michael Drayton, “Noahs Floud”, in The Muses Elizium Lately Discouered‎[3], London: John Waterson, page 108:
quote.text: The subtile shower the earth hath softned so,And with the waues, the trees tost to and fro;That the rootes loosen, and the tops downe sway,So that whole Forrests quickly swimme away.

quote.citation: 1764, Oliver Goldsmith, An History of England, in a Series of Letters from a Nobleman to his Son‎[4], London: J. Newbery, Volume 2, Letter 19, p. 159:
quote.text: The sea scurvy is attended with an universal putrefaction, the teeth loosen, old wounds that had been healed again open  […]

quote.citation: 1940, Richard Wright, Native Son‎[5], London: Jonathan Cape, published 1970, Book 3, p. 387:
quote.text: Max caught Bigger’s shoulders in a tight grip; then his fingers loosened and he sank back to the cot  […]

quote.citation: 1717, Joseph Addison, transl., Ovid’s Metamorphoses in Fifteen Books, translated by the most eminent hands‎[6], London: Jacob Tonson, Book 3, p. 99:
quote.text: At Liberty th’ unfetter’d Captive stands,And flings the loosen’d Shackles from his Hands.

quote.citation: 1796, Matthew Gregory Lewis, chapter 10, in The Monk‎[7], volume 3, London: J. Bell, page 167:
quote.text: He easily comprehended, that the noise which he had heard was occasioned by his having loosened a chain which attached the image to its pedestal.

quote.citation: 1994, J. M. Coetzee, chapter 6, in The Master of Petersburg‎[8], New York: Viking, page 55:
quote.text: Her hair is drawn back under a heavy enamelled clasp. He loosens the clasp and lays it on the table.

quote.citation: 1770, Henry Brooke, The Fool of Quality‎[9], volume 5, Dublin, page 52:
quote.text: Immediately my Shackles loosened and fell away of themselves  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To free from restraint; to set at liberty.

quote.citation: 1695, Charles Alphonse du Fresnoy, translated by John Dryden, De Arte Graphica‎[10], London: W. Rogers, page 185:
quote.text: This is an admirable Rule; a Painter ought to have it perpetually present in his Mind and Memory.  […]  it loosens his hands, and assists his understanding.

quote.citation: 1794, Ann Ward Radcliffe, chapter 5, in The Mysteries of Udolpho‎[11], volume 1, London: G.G. and J. Robinson, page 145:
quote.text: […]  Valancourt, willing to take a more extensive view of the enchanting country, into which they were about to descend, than he could do from a carriage, loosened his dogs, and once more bounded with them along the banks of the road.

quote.citation: 1876, George Eliot, Daniel Deronda‎[12], Book 1, Chapter 8:
quote.text: I thought you had more sense than  […]  to suppose that because you have fallen into a very common trouble, such as most men have to go through, you are loosened from all bonds of duty  […]

quote.citation: 1905, Edith Wharton, The House of Mirth‎[13], Book 2, Chapter 11:
quote.text: The recollection loosened a throng of benumbed sensations—longings, regrets, imaginings, the throbbing brood of the only spring her heart had ever known.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To relieve (the bowels) from constipation; to promote defecation.

quote.citation: 1626, Francis Bacon, Sylva Sylvarum: or A Naturall Historie, London: William Lee, Century 1, p. 14,[14]
quote.text: […]  Feare looseneth the Belly; because the Heat retiring inwards towards the Heart, the Gutts and other Parts are relaxed;

quote.citation: 1646, Thomas Browne, Pseudodoxia Epidemica‎[15], London: E. Dod, Book 2, Chapter 3, p. 73:
quote.text: […]  omitting the vehicle of water and honey, which is of a laxative power it selfe, the powder of some Loadstones in this dose doth rather constipate and binde, then purge and loosen the belly.

quote.citation: 1697, William Dampier, chapter 8, in A New Voyage Round the World‎[16], volume 1, London: James Knapton, page 222:
quote.text: When this Fruit [the guava] is eaten green it is binding, when ripe it is loosening.

quote.citation: 1974, Richard Adams, chapter 36, in Shardik‎[17], London: Oneworld, published 2014:
quote.text: Trying to control his breathing and the loosening of his bowels, he crouched still lower  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To create a breach or rift between (two parties).

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: I had rather lose the battle than that sisterShould loosen him and me.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, obsolete) To sail away (from the shore).

quote.citation: 1565, Arthur Golding, transl., The Eyght Bookes of Caius Iulius Cæsar conteyning his martiall exploytes in the realme of Gallia and the countries bording vppon the same‎[18], London: William Seres, Book 4:
quote.text: […]  after the .iiii. day of oure arryuall in Britayne, the eightene shyps that we spake of before, which hadde the horsemen to conuey ouer, loosened from the further hauen with a soft wynd.
